slides.headline: Build an emergency fund
slides.body: The 4-stage plan nobody spells out

slides.headline: 1. Start with ₹10,000
slides.body: Not 6 months of expenses. Just ₹10k first. A reachable number you'll actually hit.

slides.headline: 2. Get to one month
slides.body: One month of expenses covers most real emergencies. This is where panic-borrowing stops.

slides.headline: 3. Park it in a liquid fund
slides.body: Not the savings account you spend from. Separate + slightly harder to reach = it survives.

slides.headline: 4. Then aim for 3-6 months
slides.body: Only now. Building the full cushion before step 1 is why most people never start.

slides.headline: Read your payslip properly
slides.body: 4 lines that actually matter

slides.headline: 1. Gross vs net
slides.body: Gross is the headline. Net is what lands. The gap is where everything below hides.

slides.headline: 2. Your PF contribution
slides.body: Deducted, but it's yours — forced savings earning ~8%. Not a loss, a hidden asset.

slides.headline: 3. The tax slab you're in
slides.body: Know it before it's deducted. It decides whether old or new regime saves you more.

slides.headline: 4. Reimbursements vs allowances
slides.body: Allowances are taxed. Reimbursements often aren't. Structuring these cuts your tax.

slides.headline: Stock your first kitchen
slides.body: 5 basics that cook almost anything

slides.headline: 1. One good knife
slides.body: A single sharp chef's knife beats a block of dull ones. This is the tool you'll use daily.

slides.headline: 2. A heavy-bottomed pan
slides.body: Even heat, nothing burns. One pan for eggs, sabzi, and searing — buy quality once.

slides.headline: 3. Salt, oil, acid, heat
slides.body: Every dish needs these four. Master balancing them before buying 20 spices.

slides.headline: 4. Rice + dal + eggs
slides.body: The trinity. A dozen cheap, fast meals live inside just these three ingredients.

slides.headline: Over-salted your food?
slides.body: 4 fixes before you toss it

slides.headline: 1. Add a raw potato
slides.body: Drop chunks into the simmering dish. They absorb salt. Remove before serving.

slides.headline: 2. Bulk it up
slides.body: More water, more veg, more base. Dilutes the salt across a bigger volume.

slides.headline: 3. Add acid or sugar
slides.body: A squeeze of lemon or pinch of sugar masks saltiness by rebalancing the taste.

slides.headline: 4. Serve with something plain
slides.body: Rice, bread, or yogurt on the side pulls the perceived saltiness right down.

slides.headline: Guests in 20 minutes?
slides.body: Clean in this exact order

slides.headline: 1. Clear flat surfaces
slides.body: Counters, table, coffee table. Clutter reads as 'dirty' more than actual dirt does.

slides.headline: 2. The bathroom sink + mirror
slides.body: The one room guests use alone. 90 seconds here buys the most goodwill.

slides.headline: 3. Dim the lights
slides.body: Softer light hides dust instantly. Lamps over harsh overheads. Instant 'clean enough'.

slides.headline: 4. One good smell
slides.body: Coffee, a candle, citrus. Scent decides 'clean' before the eyes even look.

slides.headline: Just stained your shirt?
slides.body: The first 60 seconds decide everything

slides.headline: 1. Blot, never rub
slides.body: Rubbing drives the stain into the fibres. Press and lift with a clean cloth instead.

slides.headline: 2. Cold water for most
slides.body: Hot water sets protein stains (blood, egg, sweat). Cold first, always, when unsure.

slides.headline: 3. Grease needs dish soap
slides.body: Oil stains laugh at detergent. A drop of dish soap cuts grease before the wash.

slides.headline: 4. Never dry until it's gone
slides.body: The dryer bakes a stain in permanently. Air-dry and re-treat until it's fully out.

slides.headline: Surviving a long-haul flight
slides.body: 4 things that actually work

slides.headline: 1. Aisle for under 6 hrs, window for red-eyes
slides.body: Aisle = move freely. Window = a wall to sleep against. Pick by trip type, not habit.

slides.headline: 2. Hydrate before you board
slides.body: Cabin air is desert-dry. Drink water on the ground; you'll ask for less bad coffee up there.

slides.headline: 3. Set your watch to arrival time
slides.body: The moment you board. Your brain starts adjusting to the new zone before you land.

slides.headline: 4. Walk every 3 hours
slides.body: Not just comfort — it cuts the real clot risk of sitting still for 10+ hours.

slides.headline: Avoid tourist scams
slides.body: The same 4 show up everywhere

slides.headline: 1. The 'free' bracelet or rose
slides.body: Nothing handed to you is free. Once it's on your wrist, they demand payment. Don't accept.

slides.headline: 2. The broken taxi meter
slides.body: 'Meter not working' = inflated flat fare. Agree the price before the door shuts, or use an app.

slides.headline: 3. The overly helpful stranger
slides.body: At ATMs and ticket machines. 'Helping' is distraction while a second person watches your PIN.

slides.headline: 4. The restaurant with no prices
slides.body: No menu prices means the bill is invented for you. Prices on the menu or walk away.

slides.headline: Just moved in?
slides.body: 4 things to do in week one

slides.headline: 1. Find the mains + stopcock
slides.body: The water shut-off and fuse box. Find them calm now, not flooded at 2am later.

slides.headline: 2. Set up one working room
slides.body: Fully unpack the bedroom first. One finished space keeps you sane while chaos continues.

slides.headline: 3. Note the meter readings
slides.body: Photograph gas, water, electric on day one. Protects you from inheriting the old bill.

slides.headline: 4. Change the locks
slides.body: You don't know who has old keys. First-week job, before you trust the place.

slides.headline: Make a small room feel big
slides.body: 4 tricks that cost almost nothing

slides.headline: 1. Hang curtains high + wide
slides.body: Rod near the ceiling, wider than the window. The eye reads the whole wall as taller.

slides.headline: 2. A mirror opposite the window
slides.body: It bounces daylight and doubles the view. The single biggest 'bigger room' illusion.

slides.headline: 3. Legs on your furniture
slides.body: Sofas and beds you can see under feel lighter. Visible floor = more perceived space.

slides.headline: 4. One big piece, not many small
slides.body: A few large items feel calm and open. Lots of small ones read as cluttered and cramped.
